And he said -- he told us to go to the dormitories straight away. At that point, I saw everything blackened before my eyes, and I grabbed at Redzo's jacket, and when I came to, I was in Room 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, you referred to a person Kajin. Did you know that person's full name?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never knew it. I only knew what everybody called him, and that was Kajin, and that is how everybody knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Kajin's role in the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the commander of a shift. People talked, people said that he was a commander, and he would come. If something was underway, he would stop it. So that was how I knew that he commanded a shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him prior to your detention at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I may have come across him, but I did not know him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you see him while you were in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were three shifts, which alternated, so that I could say that it was every other day, every other, every third day, he would be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what he looked like back in 1992 when you were in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was -- he looked like an athlete. He was tall, neither thin nor fat. Shall we say an athletic type who was in good shape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, can you look around the courtroom today and see if you can see that person Kajin?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's that guy there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are-- you say you think. Does that indicate that you're not quite certain?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite concern because ten years is a long time. We've all changed, so that I cannot confirm it absolutely, but I think that it is he.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness G. Now, you referred to Zigic and Knezevic who were doing this beating and making the prisoners fight, and as they fought, hitting them with metal rods in that indent that you've referred to. Were there any regular guards involved, regular camp guards involved in that activity?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, brothers Banovic took part in it often. They were on a shift, and they beat especially Albanians whilst there were any Albanians there, but they also beat others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, on the occasion that you were called out with Redzo Grabic, were the Banovic brothers involved in that incident?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were on the side. Only Zigic and the other guy that I mentioned, whose name I don't know, took part in that. All I know about him is that he always kept -- never said anything. He only did things. And whenever they would undertake something sordid, he would be there beside Zigic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to who are you referring when you say "he"?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you about the Banovic brothers and whether they were involved in this incident that took place with Zigic and Knezevic, and you said, "They were on the side. Only Zigic and the other guy that I sometimes -- that I mentioned, whose name I don't know, took part in that. All I know about him is that he always kept -- never said anything. He only did things. And whenever they would undertake something sordid, he would be there beside Zigic." How were you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that soldier whose name I don't know. I simply do not. But he was with Zigic invariably. I don't know what his name is. I know what he looked like. He was always in a long black coat, an ordinary rifle, and he hit -- he was the one who hit me under the chin, and he kicked me with his army boot and cut the skin there. And all the others who were there, they would stand on the side. So that that time, Zigic hit me from the back, that is, on the neck and back, and this guy hit me from the front, that is, under my chin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this guy a regular guard in the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do we really need to go into this? We've been in immense detail over this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- Witness G, you're aware of an incident when you were in the camp when the Room 3 massacre took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Room 4 when it happened in Room 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case, Witness G, that, in fact, you only found out what happened after several days and after having spoken to other persons who'd witnessed the event?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First, when that incident happened in Room 3, we could not go out for two days until it was all cleaned and until blood that was there was removed. But after that, I met some people who had worked together with me and who were in Room 3 and survived, rather, Hasan Besic, specifically. I knew him because he worked for the same company as I did. He worked in the warehouse there. And he told me that people had been killed in Room 3, between 120 and 170. It is very difficult how many, and I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you back, please, Witness G, to the Banovic brothers. Were you able to tell those brothers apart?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were rather short. I couldn't really tell them apart, which one was which, because I never knew them. They were short and they had long black hair. And one of them was never without a baseball bat, and with that baseball bat, he more often than not beat prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he beat any prisoners in particular?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two prisoners. I know one of them who owned a restaurant or something at the station in Prijedor which was called Zvjezdas, and he beat him, and he was killed too. He died in Keraterm. And he also beat a fair guy whose name was Besir and who was also an Albanian. One evening he was taken away after being called out and he did not come back, so I do not know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, before the war, did you know a person by the name of Goran Grahovac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Grahovac but only superficially. He lived about a kilometre or perhaps two kilometres away from my place, and that is where his grandfather lived too. [redacted] [redacted], and he used to visit his aunt from time to time. So that -- that is how we would meet. We pass by in a car, would honk it, and I would happen to be, for instance, in my yard doing something, so we'd say hello. And I suppose at times he would walk by, but I wouldn't notice him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him while you were in Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him once. He came and they asked for me. They mentioned my full name and requested that I come out. It was around 11.00 at night. So I went out of the room, and one of the soldiers then took me up to a floor above Room 4. There was a garage there and a truck. And Goran was sitting there with five or six other soldiers. Those who were with Goran, I knew some of them by sight, and they were from Orlovci. Others I did not know. And at that point, as I stood in the middle, and they all started beating me. Then Goran began to interrogate me and he asked me about things which I simply don't understand what were they. He asked me did I know him, did I know whose son he was, and I told him I didn't. And then he swore at me and said that he was Grahovac and that Grozda was his aunt and that he often passed by my house. After --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, was this person one of the personnel, the official personnel, in the camp, or was he from outside of the camp? That is Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That person was not employed in the camp. It was the first time that I saw him there, and I think the last time that I saw him in Keraterm. I saw him yet another time but that was in Trnopolje when this was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he ask you some questions during this incident, and if so, what questions did he ask you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he -- at first he asked me some irrelevant questions, and they beat me lightly, but after sometime he said to those soldiers, "Fuck his mother, he's not talking. Take him to that room." And I started towards that room. And when I was near the door, and it had a metal door, and somebody hit me with a rod on the head, and I fell. It was all black before my eyes. I may have been a minute or two or perhaps longer unconscious. And then they ordered me, "Stand up." So I stood up and Goran then beckoned me back. And he then said to me, "Tell us where did you hide 50.000 marks and a kilogram of gold? Did you dig it into the ground somewhere?" And I told him that I didn't have that money. And that gold I had dug in somewhere because that was jewellery which belonged to my wife, to my daughter and my mother. And then he asked me, "Well, where did you bury that then?" And I described the place in detail. And he then said, "Take him to the dormitory." And a guy then saw me off to the dormitory and I went in. And just as I had somehow fitted in there, they called me out again and I came out again. And at that moment, that same guy who had escorted me to the dormitory asked me then to tell him exactly where that was buried because they didn't have much time to waste looking around for it. And I told him, "Well as I already told you, it's still there." And then I explained in great detail how he could find it because Grahovac knows where my house is. And that guard, or rather that soldier, that soldier then took me back into the room. The next day, when the dawn broke, Grahovac called me out again. And when I came out, he was sitting behind that weigh hut on a beer crate, and when I fetched up in front of him, he offered me a cigarette. And at that moment he said that he had not found the gold and that I had lied to him. And after some time and ill-treatment and questioning about I don't know what, when I said nothing because I did not have what to say, then he told me that, yes, he'd found that gold, and that he -- but that he had found it at a different place. And throughout this episode, a man called -- who was a postman, who was nicknamed Fustar, stood by. And at that moment the new commander of the camp arrived. I think he was new. He was grey-haired. He came through the gate and Fustar told Grahovac, "Get lost. Here comes the commander." And I fled to my room, number 4, and Grahovac jumped the fence and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause there for a moment, Witness G. This person Fustar, what was his role in the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was also a commander of a shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you referred to someone who was the new commander. What was his position in relation to Fustar?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that at that time, and it was after the incident in Room 3, and that man came and held a meeting or something of about ten minutes, and said that this must not happen again, ever. And that same man came that day when I had this incident where Fustar was present, and that is why I decided that he had come to replace Sikirica after the massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never had any contact with Sikirica in the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, did you ever see a person called Dusko Tadic while you were in Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him only once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was when a driver from my company was killed, and a few other lads, but that driver's nickname was Spija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was Spija killed?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Spija was battered with a metal rod or a rifle butt or a piece of wood, whatever. He was battered in a few minutes, and they called out for somebody to carry Spija. When they brought him to Room 4, we had a guy there from Trnopolje who was doing his third year or four-year course in medicine, and he tried his pulse and told us that the man was dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Spija's full name?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember his real name. I know him -- I knew him well. I've known him for some ten or 15 years, but everybody called him Spija, and he was a driver for GIK Mrakovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to this person Spija, did anything happen to his clothing after he was declared dead?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few minutes later, somebody asked -- we were locked in our room, and somebody said to take off Spija his white sneakers, because they were new, and a leather jacket that he had on. And a person took off that jacket and those sneakers and handed them over to the soldier who had asked for them. I don't know who that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness G, when the camp closed, that is Keraterm camp, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken to Trnopolje, to the camp at Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you taken there on a bus with a number of other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the Keraterm camp was disbanded and a number of buses had come. First they selected -- they called out about 120 men who were told that they would go to Omarska, and after they left, a long column of buses arrived and they began to put us on those buses, one dormitory after another. And after we were all in those buses, we were transferred to the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And eventually you were released, is that correct, Witness G?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't released. We stayed on in the camp, in Trnopolje. I stayed there some 20 days or perhaps a month. I don't know. And after that they wanted to exchange me, and that is how I arrived in Donji Vakuf, where I spent three days. After three days, they took us for exchange, and we were then exchanged in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness G.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Baly. Mr. Greaves, any cross-examination? Cross-examined by Mr. Greaves:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, can you help us, please? Before the war, were you involved in any way in politics?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, I was a member of that Communist Party of Yugoslavia, nothing else besides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since the war have you taken part, either by way of membership Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 or as being an activist, in politics?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I was in no other party after that party dissolved before the war. After that, I joined no other party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, after your final departure from the Prijedor area, did you serve at all in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now, please, about the takeover of power at the end of April 1992 by Serb-dominated authorities. It's right, isn't it, that you continued to work normally at your place of work until the 22nd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And upon ending your work on that day, it's also right that upon returning home, you were able to observe everybody working normally in the fields, minding their own business; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is how it was. People were in their fields working, going about their business. For the most part, they were in agriculture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that had been the case since the takeover of power, had it not?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it was until that day, until the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we talk of your home at that time, May 1992, was that in the village or small town of Kozarac or just outside Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in Kozarusa. This is outside of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the period leading up to the incident on the 24th of May, had there been established in that area a checkpoint which was manned by armed Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in Prijedor, and I spent all the time in Prijedor. My house was exactly between Garevci and Kozarac. I very rarely went to Kozarac. I only went there if I needed to go to a barber or if I needed to get something. I dealt with all my affairs in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so is your answer you knew of or you did not know of such a checkpoint, Witness G?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have a checkpoint where I was, and checkpoints existed only at Orlovci and in Prijedor. Perhaps in Kozarac too. I do not say that there were no checkpoints, but I do not know of them because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In due course, after the shelling had begun in your area and a command or an order came down that you should be taken to a safe place, was it your understanding that that order had come from the Serbian high command?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- this was our understanding, that this was the order. And this neighbour of mine came to me. His house was about 200 metres away from me. He told me that the order came from the command, that we should all go to -- in front of the local commune at Kozarusa and from there we would be bused to some safe place where there was no shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having been placed on buses, you were -- can I just clarify this? Men of military age were put on one side of the bus and women and children and other people were put on the opposite side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on the bus?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken to Trnopolje. Or was it just men on the bus going to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were only men in some buses, and on other buses they placed women, children, and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so just again to clarify, the men on the buses were men aged principally between 16 and 60 years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was a separation maintained in terms of accommodation during your stay at Trnopolje, until the women and children were taken away or released; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were separated for about three days, until more space opened up in Trnopolje. Women and children were in the school building and the gymnasium at Trnopolje, and the men were outside and in some old hall. After a few days, when we were too many, nobody paid any attention any more who was with whom. So we were all mixed, men, women, children, so that the families could visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suspect the witness, as well as do I find it slightly disconcerting seeing as he's got to peer around the ELMO at me. I wonder whether it could be moved, please, because I can see that he's having to lean back from the microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the ELMO be adjusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Push it back, please, yes. I'm not planning to use it. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when this mixing took place, was that simply something that the detainees did for themselves without reference to the people who were running Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this simply happened spontaneously because there was no room either in the school building or in this hall. We were forced to be outside. And then, of course, people started looking around for their wives. And at that point, nobody prohibited us. We were separated for about three days, and then later on we all mixed in together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that partly brought about because large numbers of people were arriving each day, up to a thousand?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that is why this mingling took place in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, were you able to conclude from what you saw of how the camp was organised in terms of what we have just been talking about, were you able to conclude that in fact there wasn't a great deal of organisation taking place from the authorities who had opened the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no organisation because there weren't enough of those who were guards, and there were too many of us who were behind that fence, who were in the school building, and whatever that other building was. I wasn't going there so often. I didn't know. So we were just trying to find our way, whichever way we could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I turn now, please, to the departure of your family from Trnopolje? They were released in mid-June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably it was so. I don't know the exact time. They were taken to Banja Luka. They were put in cars and taken there. There they waited for about three hours until the train moved along. Then they were transferred to -- some were to Doboj and from there they had to go on foot until they reached Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it's travel to Zagreb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a period of time, my wife and children went to Zagreb, and then from there, to my sister's place in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your family's release was not unique, was it? This is what happened to all -- most, if not all, of the families who were in Trnopolje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened -- I think that this is what happened. I was in another camp. I wasn't there. But from what my wife told me, some 2.000 people were put on this train and this is how they arrived at Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there people left behind after the families had departed, according to your information?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of women and children and men remained there, and everything was mixed. There were older and younger people there. I know that when I came from Keraterm after it was closed and arrived at Trnopolje for the first time I found them there. Some had remained in Trnopolje and the others had left in this one, if I can call it, a convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to Keraterm, did you see any of those who had been guards at Trnopolje at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was different staff at Keraterm. I cannot say that I saw the same guards from Trnopolje in Keraterm. I'm not sure that I saw any of them there. I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to move on to another topic. I don't know at what time Your Honour wants to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take the break at ten minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thanks very much. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, can you help me, please? You were taken in due course to the barracks at Prijedor, and you've described one of those people as being obviously from the military police. Was that the case in respect of all of those who were in charge of guarding you at Prijedor barracks, that they were members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No some were in uniform without belts. I mentioned one who was quite short, was wearing a fur hat with a Kokarda and was wearing some dark clothes. So there weren't only policemen there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were other people who were detained at the same time as you, and if so, how many, at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, in room where I was, we were about eight, plus\minus one person, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were those eight or thereabouts, were they all men of military age?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were all of the age up to 50, approximately. Except for this one boy who was underaged, the son of this Lovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that you were asked about in particular whether you had had weapons, and whether you knew of the whereabouts of Green Berets, and when you were unable to provide him with any answers, it was that which set him off beating you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. He started beating us and he repeated the same thing three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "beating us," were you all together, these eight people, however many there were, at the same time being beaten, or was this being done separately?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself, Redzo Grabic and Mujkanovici were beaten together. That was while we were being brought to the barracks, the three of us, and then they beat the others separately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just on the topic which you were asked about, before you had been detained at all and taken to Trnopolje, had you been aware of any military activity at all along the road from Kozarusa to Prijedor, Witness G?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except that we were told, that is what we heard on the radio, that there would be a military column coming from Bihac going to Banja Luka, and people were told to stay put in order not to obstruct the column as they were -- would be passing. And this is all I know about those things. This was before the beginning, before the start, around 2.30, when the shooting first started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been aware before your detention, either from your own observation or from being told about it, of Muslims arming themselves and preparing in any way to fight with or resist the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you specifically but I don't think you could say so. When the war in Croatia started, we were together with those neighbours who were there with us. They were simply upset. They thought that these HOS people were cross over from Croatia, this is how they called them. And then when Ranko Vlacina and with Bobo Vlacina, Ilja Vlacina, the four or five of us were always there together. Their houses were the first ones and then our houses were next. So we were there. We did not have any weapons. And they were our neighbours so we never counted of what later happened it would happen, because their three or four houses were amongst our own homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves, I think we will now take the break for 20 minutes. Witness G, you're reminded not to discuss your evidence with anybody during the adjournment, and that includes the members of the Prosecution team. To ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just mention that there is a matter that I would like to raise on behalf of all the Defence at the end of today, which will take between five and ten minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think for that purpose then, we may break five minutes before five.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, I want now to turn very quickly to the time when you were delivered to Keraterm by the man you've described as Tyson: The other people who were there as taking part in this beating, you've described someone I think with the name of Sengin or Sengin [pronounced phonetically]. Was he somebody called Jasmin Ramadanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that he was -- that everybody called him Sengin. What his real name is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was the man Tyson who effectively organised or said to Zigic that you were to be singled out or people in your group were to be singled out for special treatment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tyson told Zigic that those four were for special treatment, and for another four, he said nothing. It only applied to those four, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 Sengin, the machine-gunner, and the two Jakupovic brothers. The four of them were intended for special treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Tyson was not, and was not at any time, on the camp staff, was he?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time. He turned us over and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to an occasion when Zigic was involved in beating a group, I think, of some 22 or so people sometime before the 14th of July. It's right, isn't it, that that incident concluded when Kajin came to the gate where the scales were and told Zigic to stop what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also right that upon being so ordered, Zigic did stop beating the people?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He stopped at the very same moment and said, "Just beat it to your room."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that on at least one occasion or more a doctor came to Keraterm and examined prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A doctor came once, a Macedonian, and I've just remembered his name, Elenkov. I knew because I had to go see him several times about my driving licence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, you were interrogated. Can you recall what the date of your interrogation was, please?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. I do not know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it have been about one month after your arrival at Room 2 at Keraterm? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could be. Perhaps a little less. Between 15 and 30 days, but I really cannot pinpoint the date because I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you escorted to the interrogation by one of the guards from Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One called out -- called me out and said that it was my turn for interrogation and took me to the building. The interrogations took place on the upper floor. There I was taken over by another soldier and escorted me to the room and then the interrogation continued there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that the only role that the guard performed during the interrogation process, simply to escort you to and from the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was his only role, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone or have the microphones brought closer to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness G, please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, the questions you were asked you've told us a little about. Were they particularly interested in whether you or your family had been involved in the military?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what they wanted to know. I know what they asked me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in that connection, without mentioning either his relationship to you or his name, one of your relatives was a member of the Bosnian 7th Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently learn that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subsequently, yes, when we left the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that because when you were exchanged, it became clear to you that you had been specifically requested for exchange because of your relationship to this person?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not realise that until I arrived in Travnik, and afterwards they told me that there were some captured Serbs and that was why they had exchanged us because they had asked for me and for two brothers to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the person who was interrogating -- to go back to your interrogation, did you know the person who was interrogating you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, the people who were involved in the interrogations, they were not part of the camp staff, were they?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not, because they would come every day when there were interrogations. They would come to the camp, climb upstairs to those interrogation rooms, and they would spend their time there, and once the interrogations were over, they would leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the consequences of your interrogation were that you were moved from where you were to Room 4; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. It was a kind of a custom. After the interrogation, above Room -- from Room 2 people would be transferred to Room 1. When the Room 1 was filled up, we were transferred to Room 4, after every interrogation those who had been through that and finished with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move please to the Room 3 incident. It's right, isn't it, that the people who perpetrated that were, according to what you learnt, soldiers from outside the camp, not employed as camp staff?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Difficult to say that because we were locked up in our rooms. However, two trucks with men arrived, and who did that, I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not able to see -- you were locked into the room so that nobody in the room that you were in could see anything of what was going on? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not quite. A person who was near the door could see, since the door to Room 4 was painted and the men scraped off the colour and they could peep through and see what went on outside. But only one person, not more of them. And when it all happened, it was night-time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this correct, Witness G, that for some two days in total after that incident, you, the people in your room, were not let out at all?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not leave our room, and I'm sure that other people from other rooms did not come out either until the whole place was cleaned after what had happened. And when we did come out, we could still see that the concrete and the wall were still bloody, and there were countless holes from either machine-gun projectiles or whatever. One could see it in the walls, which were brick walls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so that we can establish it with certainty, the period during which you were not let out of the rooms was the day immediately following the night of the massacre, is that correct, and the day after that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. We did not come out the following day either. We had to use a kind of a barrel, a tin barrel in the room, and that was what was put there for us to relieve ourselves in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the next time that you emerge from the room is then the morning following those two days?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was a morning when we were let out to go to the WC, stretch our legs a little, and we could stand next to the wall because there was a small grassy lawn and we could stand there up to the path. We were not allowed to cross the path.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The incident involving the gentleman who owned the ice cream and cake shop at Prijedor station, Zvjezdas or Zvjezdas, is this right, that the motive for ill-treating him was to try and extort money or valuables from him?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that. I cannot say it because I do not know what the motive was. I know they were cursing him and swearing at his Albanian mother and beating him. As for money or something, I cannot tell you because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In general, the Banovic brothers, was their motivation in ill-treating people to try and extort money from them? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I know nothing about it, so I cannot really say yes or no. I do not know what the reason was. I know that those two Albanians were beaten to death, Besim and that Zvjezdas. I know that they were taken out quite a number of times and beaten with a baseball bat. Why, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, as far as -- you've told us that you had no direct contact with a man called Sikirica. Is this correct, that in regard to information concerning him, you had to rely on information from other people?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody said, and guards also said, because we all had friends or colleagues or school fellows, people who were quite good colleagues, and they would come into the dormitories and talk to their colleagues, so they themselves said that Sikirica was the camp commander. I don't have a paper to that effect, nor did I get some order. I had no way of finding out whether that was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The new commander's name, was that Marinko Sandzak?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what his name is. I can only describe him to you. I know that he had grey hair and that he was slightly over 50. I don't know what his name is, absolutely, I just don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If Your Honour would just give me a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know anything of where the new commander came from or where he worked?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know and I do not know where he came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, does the name Zivko Knezevic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zivko Knezevic? I heard that he was in the police station, that he was the chief of the police station or something, but I just don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you now, please, about somebody called Bajazit Jakupovic? Is that a name with which you're familiar?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware during your stay in Keraterm of the presence of somebody who was a military pilot, who was a detainee?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I once saw a guy and everybody said that he was a military pilot, that he was a pilot for the army, and I think that his name was Jakupovic or something, but I'm not sure. He was in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the only pilot of whom you were aware at the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the only one I knew. I don't know about any others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware that he had gone to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know. I don't know what happened to him. I know the man was -- he seemed to have become unhinged. He would come out when he was not supposed to and - I don't know - was around there. But what happened to him, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Witness G, during either of your stays at Trnopolje, did you see personally Dusko Sikirica at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Trnopolje, no, I did not see him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness G. Hang on a second. Sorry. Would you wait a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There's one point I had forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness G, when the Keraterm was closed, it's right, isn't it, that two buses took prisoners to Omarska, and they were in total about 120? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes. About 120. And they said they were going to Omarska. Where they went, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Greaves. Mr. Rodic. Cross-examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness G. During your examination-in-chief, you said that you were going to work all the way until 22 May 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to work until 22 May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether other people did go to work in the month of May? Did they go to work at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, they did, but some people did not because there wasn't enough work, some people, that is, but I don't think that that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, you mentioned that very day that there was a checkpoint to which you came and you saw different people wearing different uniforms there. What I'm interested in is that period May to August of that year. Did you see different uniforms that people were wearing at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were different types of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was all in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the Prijedor area and that checkpoint at Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned 24th of May and how you heard on Radio Prijedor that a military column was moving along the Prijedor-Banja Luka road and that it was asked that it be allowed to pass in an unobstructed way, did you learn later where it was obstructed or not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The column never reached Kozarusa, where we lived. The shooting started before they reached that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the first 12 days that you spent at Trnopolje, can you tell me whether you were interrogated by anyone there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not interrogated in Trnopolje by anyone at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me something about the security of Trnopolje, the area where you were at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be hard to say anything about the security. There were guards there. They were walking about. There was some low fence. I don't know what it was, some kind of a sports field or something. They were around there, but there wasn't a large number of them, so occasionally they allowed us to go and pick up some corn or something to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, they allowed you to leave the perimeter, to leave that compound, if we can call it that way?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were individuals who knew these guards well. They were either school friends or colleagues from work or someone like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned your transfer to the Prijedor barracks, you mentioned a name of that military policeman as being nicknamed Tyson, the person who beat you. Can you tell me whether anybody tried to prevent him in doing this?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody prevented him from beating us, but after the third time, when he went out and said, "I'll be back in a minute," and when he told us that he would cut our throats if we did not tell him where the weapons were, a minute later he came back with a knife in his hand. At that point, a military policeman entered the room from outside. He was tall, about 30 years old, and he told Tyson to go back to the room, and he took to us the prison that was across from the toilet where we were being beaten - that prison only had bars - and he locked us in and took the key with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, this soldier, this military policeman who -- the military policemen like Tyson, were they regular policemen or something else?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Tyson was wearing only a belt, and the other policeman who defended us, who locked us up, he had both a belt around the waist and another belt or strap across the shoulder. I don't know if they were the same unit or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were interrogated three times in the barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who it was that interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time, Tyson interrogated and beat us. Then we were taken to the room, but I cannot tell you the names. I didn't know these people. They were only wearing military uniforms. That's all I know about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't need to try to push your memory. I only ask you to tell me what you know. When you were taken to these offices -- and people there, did they have any military ranks? Could you distinguish them from the military policemen in any way?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not notice any rank insignia on them. They were just in the SMB uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During these interrogations, were these individuals making any notes, taking notes of the questions -- of the answers that you were giving them?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably did, because they had a pen and paper on their desks. It's hard for me to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the barracks, you were taken in a van to Keraterm. Did this van have any markings of the military police on it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was a civilian van. There were no military markings on it. It looked like a civilian vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Keraterm, did Tyson call this group a group for special treatment? Did he identify them as such?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, there were eight of us that -- who arrived, and those four he designated as the ones for special treatment and not the four of us. So only four were singled out for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Samir Sistek?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name does not ring any bells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Keraterm, you were placed in Room 2. Can you describe in some detail where exactly you were staying, given the room?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at rear to the right. There was a wire -- a fenced-in part where there was machinery, so that was fenced off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, as you look down into the room from the entrance door to the place where you were, what would be the distance, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been six to seven metres, I couldn't give you. It changed too. At one day, you were in one place, and the next day, wherever you are able to find a spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the situation where you were in that position in number 2 where you found a spot, between that spot and the door, how many men approximately were there? I don't ask you an accurate number.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of people. I think that there were a total of about 400 of us in that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a barrel where you relieved yourself in that room?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, it wasn't there. I don't remember it, because we were let out to the toilet, which was behind Rooms 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this barrel brought in at a later time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that after the incident, a barrel was brought into Room 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your arrival, who called out the Jakupovic brothers and Sengin that same night?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Zigic who called them out, and he also beat them, and obviously the other company that was with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a person who frequently came with Zigic and who did not speak much, and you said that you did not know his name. Is his description something like this? That he was of medium build, short, dark hair, maybe a bit longer, going down to his shoulders, darker complexion?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I remember, he was medium height, he was thinner rather than fat, and as far as his hair cut, I really wouldn't be able to tell you. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On one occasion you mentioned a person who was missing an arm, who was coming to the camp. Do you know that his name was Mico Kobas?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his name. I only saw him once. He was down there at Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that he brought some disinfectants to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion he did, because we had lice, so we -- he brought it for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they took you from Room 2 to the upper floor to be interrogated, did the person who interrogated you make any notes on the basis of conversation that you had?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was writing something. I saw him with a pen and paper while he interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that the investigators were not part of the Keraterm security, and given their comings and goings in the camp, can you give us an assessment, were these investigators hierarchically higher up than the guards in the Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard for me to tell you. From what I know, they were coming, interrogating, and then leaving in the evening. Then they would come back the next morning when there were interrogations. Sometimes interrogations would stop and then several days later they would come back. And perhaps they were involved in some other work meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you moved to Room 4, can you tell me approximately how many people were there in that room at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe between 300 and 400.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, the same question as I asked you about Room 2: Where was your exact position in that room?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you enter the room, I was to the right. I was -- there were the people to the left and people to the right. I was a bit -- I was at a place that was between mid-point and a bit closer to the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you express that in metres?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps four metres away from the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Drago Tokmadzic also -- a policeman, also with you in that room?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Drago Tokmadzic, the policeman, was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was placed in that room, I don't know how long he was there, but one night he was called out, taken out, and about within ten minutes, he was killed. He just -- they just told us to come and carry him in, and we brought him in and the next day he was taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who had called him out?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard for me to say at this point because quite a bit of time has passed by, and you're not always able to tell by voice who was calling people out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you recall whether somebody called him from outside or a person came in to call him out?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it -- somebody came to the door and they called him from the doorway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did Grahovac also beat you on that same night?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the same night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it in relation to that night, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grahovac beat me one day before the closing of Keraterm. When Keraterm was disbanded, one day before that, he beat me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was present when you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Grahovac and six men with him. I don't know their names, but I knew some of them because they were from Orlovci, and I knew them from -- in passing, from when I was going to work and passed through there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you go back to the room?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all this, one of the soldiers from the group escorted me, that is from the group who were -- of soldiers who were with Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means it wasn't one of the regular guards from the shift?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't -- Grahovac came with this crew of his. There were six or seven of them. I saw them for the first time on that occasion and it was also the last time that I saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, to give us time to deal with the matter that Mr. Greaves has intimated he wishes to have us consider, we will have the witness leave now. Witness G, you may leave now and return tomorrow morning at 9.30. During the break you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including members of the Prosecution team. Please escort the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. It arises out of a question that Your Honour asked of the witness yesterday afternoon concerning the defendant Sikirica. Your Honour, what you said -- and I've got copies here of the three relevant passages I'm going to draw Your Honours' attention to. I'm afraid I don't have the French version because we don't yet have a French transcript of any of the hearings thus far. And there are two for my learned friends as well. Your Honour will see there's an extract from page 1597. At that point, Your Honour lifted what appeared to us on the Defence side of the room to be a copy of the summary of the witness who was giving evidence and asked the question:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe you gave evidence that after the second massacre, which was the day after the first, you saw him when the bodies were being removed. And you then went on to ask him whether he had seen Sikirica at any time after that and prior to his leaving. Your Honour, the answers that had been given in relation to those two matters are set out in the two extracts at 1578 and 1580. The effect of the first passage is that the witness was saying, in relation to Simo Drljaca and Sikirica, in particular in relation to Sikirica, at line 23:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the presence of any other dignitaries?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that accompanying him was Sikirica, but I cannot assert that. I think that he was. Over the page:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it just the two of them, the person you think may have been Sikirica or Drljaca, or were there yet other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 people with them? And the second passage relates to the period after the second massacre. Counsel for the Prosecution asked the witness -- was looking for the answer that Your Honour was anticipating, but it didn't come and he quite properly then desisted from asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What line is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Line 10 of page 1581, which is -- just begins at the top there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see who was present during the loading of that second truck on the second day?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We could not see it then, because we were not allowed to leave the rooms. And then the counsel for the Prosecution goes on and asks about Jasmin Causevic. So the effect of the evidence is there is no evidence, in our submission, that Sikirica, according to this witness, was present during the loading of the bodies. The question that Your Honour asked was:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe you gave evidence that after the second massacre, which was the day after the first, you saw him when the bodies were being removed. Now, our concerns are these, and I speak, I hope, for all Defence counsel, that if a witness is to have evidence put to him, it should be evidence, not that which comes from a summary which is inconsistent with the evidence actually given. Second concern we have is the use to which these summaries are to be put. The summaries, in our submission, are no more than a road-map which sets out where the Prosecutor plans to go with the witness. Once the evidence is completed, the summary becomes a document of precious little value, for it is not evidence, it's not an exhibit, and the evidence only comes from the witness box or through documents which are admitted and authenticated. We respectfully express that concern because if the questions that Your Honours are going to ask are going to come from the summaries which are inconsistent with evidence actually given, it is, we submit, unfair if the questions being put to witnesses are prefaced by that which is not evidence. And on this particular point, it's an important difference because the evidence is quite clear. We submit there is no evidence that Sikirica was present. So we would just like to express our very deep concerns that it's not the summary which is to be used as evidence, it is the evidence which is to be used as evidence in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Two -- yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I must say that I take the view that the summaries that are provided are exactly for the purpose that the Court asked, and that is to give an indication as to what use -- or where the Prosecution is going with the witness. But in fairness, I must say that this Court is very much entitled to ask questions on its own in order to clarify issues, and with the greatest of respect, I see no difficulty whatever with the Court asking the question that it did at page 1597, asking the witness to clarify whether he saw him at any time at Keraterm. And as a matter of fact, the witness did come up with an answer, that he said he remembered the issue quite well, and then gave his explanation. With respect, I don't see a problem. Maybe I'm missing something, but we are preparing these summaries on the basis of anticipated evidence based on the statements that we have taken and proofing sessions, and at the Court's request, we've provided those. And my understanding is that the Court is quite entitled to ask questions on its own of the witnesses, to clarify issues. This is not exactly the complete adversarial system that perhaps might be exactly the same in everyone's national jurisdictions. It's a system that is unique to this Tribunal and it's a search for the truth, and the Court does have the right to play an active role in clarifying issues that are of concern to it. Those are my views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think we need to hear any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I just want to say this, Your Honour. I'm not disputing that Your Honours have the right to ask questions, nor am I disputing that the question you actually asked was a perfectly proper one. What I am disputing is that you put to the witness, before doing so, something which was not the evidence and which was extracted from the summary. The two things are different. It risks, in the future, a witness -- something unfair happening with the witness if you ask a question which is based on the summary but which is not in accord with the evidence. That's the problem I face. I don't have a problem with Your Honours -- indeed, I encourage Your Honours to ask questions. I'm quite happy with that, and that is entirely proper. It was the use of the summary incorrectly in accordance with the evidence that was the matter of concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't agree that the summary was used at all, and the sole issue is whether there was evidence, and I'll use the break this evening to examine the matter and make a comment on it tomorrow morning. I don't think the Chamber needs to be lectured about the use of the summary. It's a truism that the summary is not evidence, and the sole issue is whether there was evidence. We will look at the issue this evening, and tomorrow we'll make a comment on it. We stand adjourned until 9.30 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: If I could be recognised Your Honour. Your Honour, if I could be recognised for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, because Mr. Greaves purported to speak on your behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: On a different issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have another matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I noticed there is a practice here that when the objection is being raised and the Court is questioning and asking the counsel what is the substance of the objection, the translation goes on and the witness is being basically cued in what the proper answer is, or perhaps when the Court asked where the examination is leading to. In a jurisdiction where I am practising and Your Honours, most of you are practising -- actually, two of you are practising, that calls for a side-bar conference because we do indeed have a jury. And I understand, since we do not have a jury but we still do have a witness, and I would respectfully ask when such matters are being raised, because as you see that this is indeed a delicate trial, if we possibly enhance the fairness and perhaps, you know, just exclude the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucicevic. We stand adjourned until 9.30.
